# The classical continuity of electronic globalization 1

Routledge eBooks. Published: 2019-04-05. Book chapter. 0 citations.

## Abstract

History does not repeat itself, but it helps us understand the present. Brushing aside Niels Bohr’s warning against predicting the future, we may perhaps even prognosticate with caution. Just as the Industrial Revolution lifted masses of Europeans out of poverty, so did the manufacturing globalization create a Chinese middle class. The digital revolution is doing the same the world over. Social changes will be unavoidable, since one cannot move forward while simultaneously standing still. Nothing impedes progress as much as ignorance, and the massive surge in information flow will increase standards of living and lower social and economic inequities. And this will happen not because it is something marvellous and new, but because it is a new manifestation of a historical continuum. The commentary in the Addendum revisits some thoughts published in Decision in 2009 on the nature and possible repercussions of the global spread of ICTs. The central hypothesis stands, viz. technologies are unlikely to produce economic headwinds for richer nations and tailwinds for the poorer ones on balance. A few of the arguments are extended in light of recent developments regarding privacy and security .
